## Overview

The Tanka, also called Boat Dwellers, Boat People, or *Shuishangren* (水上人), are an unrecognized ethnic group in China. They traditionally lived on boats and junks in coastal parts of Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Hainan, Zhejiang, cities along the Yangtze river, Hong Kong, and Macau. Boat Dwellers also live along the Grand Canal and in river and bay regions including the Xin'an River, Fuchun River, Lanjiang River, Min River Mouth, Pearl River Mouth, and Macau Bay. Many now live onshore, while some older people continue to live on boats and fish. They speak varieties of Yue Chinese; Boat Dwellers in Fujian speak Fuzhounese. Their folk-cultural significance in the sources lies chiefly in boat-based settlement, fishing, social history, language, and relationships with southern Chinese populations.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Boat Dwellers traditionally lived on boats and junks. In Hong Kong, Walter Schofield described them in 1937 as living in boats hauled ashore or in more or less boat-shaped huts, including at Shau Kei Wan and Tai O. Some built markets or villages on the shore, while others continued to live on their junks or boats. Those with small boats who could not fish far out to sea gathered in bays like floating villages.

## Music & performance

 The article identifies Sinn Sing Hoi as a composer from Macau and mentions a poem by the Chinese poet Wu Li about Boat Dwellers supplying fish to the Portuguese.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe social exclusion from Cantonese and Hakka celebrations: Boat Dweller people were barred from those celebrations.

## Foodways

The sources state that Boat Dwellers traditionally pursued fishing and that Cantonese often bought fish from them. Boat Dwellers supplied fish to the Portuguese in Macau as well. Historical classifications referred to “the fish-Tan, the oyster-Tan, and the wood-Tan,” based on livelihood.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources mention several historical and literary representations of the Boat Dwellers. Chinese myths claimed that animals were ancestors of the Barbarians, and some ancient Chinese sources said that water snakes were ancestors of the Boat Dwellers. A poem by Wu Li mentions Boat Dwellers supplying fish to the Portuguese. Literature in Macau addressed love affairs and marriage between Boat Dweller women and Portuguese men, including *A-Chan, A Tancareira* by Henrique de Senna Fernandes.

## Language & religion

The Boat Dwellers speak a variety of Yue Chinese similar in phonology to Cantonese. The sources state that Boat Dwellers living in Fujian speak Fuzhounese and that their original language had largely disappeared from daily use by the early 20th century. Maurice Freedman wrote that their spoken tongue was increasingly indistinguishable from regional Cantonese by the late 19th century. The sources describe several pronunciation features, including changes affecting /œ/, /y/, /kʷ/, final -m and -p, and /n/.
